lines.text: GIFT Nifty points to a gap-up of about 120 points after the US rally. FPIs sold ₹2,000 crore in cash yesterday; DIIs bought most of it back.
Breadth was weak, though. Three heavyweights held the index up while the mid caps bled.
So the rally is narrow. I'm not chasing the open. If we gap up into 24,800, I'd rather trim than add.
Noted. There's a call wall at 25,000, so that's the ceiling everyone is watching.

questions.q: Why doesn't the PM want to chase the open?
options: Few stocks are rising: breadth is weak
FPIs bought heavily in cash yesterday
GIFT Nifty points to a gap-down
The desk has no positions at all
questions.why: Weak breadth means a handful of heavyweights carried the index, which makes the rally fragile.

questions.q: What does the call wall at 25,000 suggest?
options: Writers expect the index to stay below it
The index will open above 25,000
Puts at 25,000 are very expensive
The exchange caps the index at 25,000
questions.why: Heavy call writing at a strike is read as resistance: the writers are betting the index stays below it.

lines.text: Our big IT long reported last night: revenue a touch light, margins beat, and they raised guidance.
What's priced in? The stock ran 9% into the number.
The straddle implied a 5% move, and the street expected the guidance raise. A lot of it is priced in.
Then it's a sell-the-news risk. Take some off the table at the open and keep the core.

questions.q: Why might the stock fall even on decent results?
options: It ran up 9% and the raise was expected
The straddle implied no move at all
Revenue beat by a wide margin
The company cut its guidance
questions.why: When a stock has rallied into results the street already expected, good news can trigger selling.

questions.q: What does the PM want done at the open?
options: Sell part of the position, keep the rest
Sell the whole position before the call
Buy more because margins beat
Hedge it with a short straddle
questions.why: 'Take some off the table' means bank part of the gain; 'keep the core' means hold the rest.

lines.text: The RBI announces at 10. Consensus is a hold, but two members voted for a cut last time.
What does the book look like into it?
You're long bank stocks and long government bonds. A hawkish surprise hurts both.
Then I'll go flat into the event on the bonds and keep the banks. One bet on the RBI is enough.

questions.q: Why is Risk worried?
options: Both positions lose if the RBI sounds hawkish
The banks and the bonds hedge each other
Consensus expects a surprise rate hike
The book is short banks into the policy
questions.why: Bank stocks and bond prices both tend to fall when rates look set to stay higher, so the two positions are one bet.

questions.q: What does 'go flat into the event on the bonds' mean?
options: Close the bond position before the decision
Keep the bonds and hedge the bank stocks
Double the bond position before 10 am
Buy bonds only after the RBI cuts rates
questions.why: Going flat into an event means closing the position so the announcement can't hurt it.

lines.text: Weekend news: crude is up 6% on supply worries. Expect oil marketing and paint stocks to open weak.
Asia has opened risk-off, so India VIX will jump at the open.
We're short gamma through the straddles. What's the gap risk?
A 1% gap costs the book about ₹12 lakh. I'd buy wings before the open, not after.

questions.q: Why is the PM asking about gap risk?
options: A short-gamma book loses on a big open move
A long straddle loses if prices gap
Gaps only matter for cash shares
The exchange limits gaps on Mondays
questions.why: Short straddles are short gamma: a big jump either way costs more than the premium earned.

questions.q: What does the trader suggest?
options: Buy far OTM options to cap the loss
Sell more straddles at the open
Close the book after the open
Short crude oil futures as a hedge
questions.why: Buying wings means buying options further out than the ones sold, which caps the worst case.

lines.text: FPIs have sold for nine straight sessions and are heavily short index futures.
Who's on the other side? Domestic funds keep buying every dip.
Exactly. With SIP money coming in every month, the pain trade is higher, not lower.
Then I don't want to be short into that. Bring the net down to flat, not negative.

questions.q: Why does the strategist call a rally the pain trade?
options: Many FPIs are short, so a rally hurts them most
Domestic funds are short and would lose
A rally would stop SIP inflows
Rallies always follow nine down days
questions.why: The pain trade is the move that hurts the most people given how they are positioned.

questions.q: What does the PM decide?
options: Cut net exposure to about zero, not go short
Go heavily net short with index futures
Add more longs to ride the rally
Close every position before the open
questions.why: 'Bring the net down to flat, not negative' means reduce net exposure to zero without turning net short.

lines.text: Rollovers are running behind last month: 62% with two days to go.
Is it longs or shorts not rolling?
Mostly longs. Open interest is falling as the price falls: long unwinding.
So there's no fresh conviction on the long side. Keep sizes small until the new series settles.

questions.q: What does 'long unwinding' tell you?
options: Buyers are closing positions as the price falls
New shorts are being added on the fall
Buyers are adding as the price falls
Shorts are buying back into a rally
questions.why: Falling price with falling open interest means existing longs are getting out.

questions.q: Why does the PM keep sizes small?
options: Fewer longs are carrying positions forward
Rollover costs have doubled this month
The exchange has cut the lot size
Shorts are rolling at a record pace
questions.why: Low rollover by longs shows little appetite to stay long into next month.

lines.text: The new signal has a Sharpe of 1.9 over ten years, long-short in the Nifty 500.
Before costs?
Yes, gross. It turns over about 40% of the book a week.
Then show me net. At that turnover I doubt it survives costs. And check it against plain 12-month momentum; it may be a factor in disguise.

questions.q: Why does the head of research ask for net numbers?
options: High turnover could eat the edge in costs
Gross Sharpe is always overstated by half
Net numbers remove the market's beta
SEBI requires net figures in reviews
questions.why: A strategy that trades 40% of its book a week pays a lot in costs, which can wipe out a gross edge.

questions.q: What does 'a factor in disguise' mean here?
options: It may just be the known momentum factor
It is a factor that only works in secret
It hides its trades from other funds
It works only on unnamed stocks
questions.why: A new signal that mostly repeats a well-known factor adds little to a book that already holds it.

lines.text: This short-term reversal rule had no losing year since 2012. Sharpe of 4.
That's too good to be true. What universe?
Today's Nifty 100 members, on daily closes.
There's your problem: survivorship bias. And you trade at the same close you used for the signal. Use point-in-time members and trade the next open.

questions.q: What is wrong with using today's Nifty 100 members?
options: It leaves out the stocks that dropped out
It adds too many illiquid small caps
It counts the index's dividends twice
It mixes NSE and BSE prices
questions.why: Today's members are the survivors. Stocks that fell out of the index, often after falling, are missing from the test.

questions.q: Why trade at the next open instead of the same close?
options: You can't know the close before it prints
The next open always has lower costs
The close is not a real traded price
Exchanges don't allow trades at the close
questions.why: Using the close to decide and trading at that same close is look-ahead bias.

lines.text: Here are the quintiles. Top minus bottom is 1.1% a month.
It isn't monotonic, though. Buckets two to four are flat; it's all in the bottom bucket.
The bottom bucket is mostly small caps that crashed.
Which we can't short overnight without futures or stock borrowing. The tradable spread is much smaller. Try it inside the F&O stocks.

questions.q: Why is the reviewer unhappy with the buckets?
options: All the spread comes from one extreme bucket
Returns rise steadily bucket by bucket
The top bucket has negative returns
There are too few buckets to judge
questions.why: A good signal's returns step up across the buckets; a spread from one bucket is weaker evidence.

questions.q: Why test it inside the F&O stocks?
options: Their shorts can be held through futures
F&O stocks have no trading costs
F&O stocks never crash
Only F&O stocks can be sorted
questions.why: In India an overnight short in a cash stock needs stock borrowing or a single-stock future, which only F&O stocks have.

lines.text: I tested 240 combinations of lookback and threshold and picked the best.
What do the neighbours look like?
The best is 23 days. At 20 or 26 it's close to zero.
Knife-edge, and too many knobs. Fix one parameter from a reason, walk it forward, and deflate the Sharpe for 240 tries.

questions.q: What does 'knife-edge' mean here?
options: It works only at one exact lookback
It works at every lookback tested
It is about to hit its stop-loss
It trades only near the day's highs
questions.why: A robust result holds across nearby settings; one that vanishes when nudged is probably overfit.

questions.q: Why deflate the Sharpe ratio?
options: Picking the best of 240 tries flatters it
Sharpe ratios fall with inflation
The strategy pays high taxes
The returns were measured in dollars
questions.why: The best of many tries looks good by luck alone; the deflated Sharpe ratio corrects for the number of trials.

lines.text: The fund made 22% last year against 15% for the Nifty.
With a beta of 1.4, though. Regress it and the alpha is about one percent.
So most of it was just beta?
Yes. In a 15% year, a beta of 1.4 gives you 21% before any skill.

questions.q: How much of the 22% does a beta of 1.4 explain in a 15% year?
options: About 21%
About 15%
About 7%
About 1.4%
questions.why: 1.4 × 15% = 21%, leaving about 1% of alpha.

questions.q: What does 'just beta' mean?
options: The return came mostly from market exposure
The fund beat the market with stock picks
The fund was hedged against the market
The return came from currency moves
questions.why: When beta explains nearly all of a return, it came from being long the market, not from skill.

lines.text: The IC is 0.05 on one-day forward returns, 0.02 at five days, and nothing at twenty.
So it's a fast signal. Can we trade it daily without giving it all away in costs?
With a no-trade band, turnover halves and we keep most of the IC.
Good. Paper trade it for a month before any capital.

questions.q: What does the IC pattern say?
options: It predicts the next day, not the next month
It gets stronger the longer you hold
It predicts only twenty-day returns
It has no predictive power at all
questions.why: The information coefficient is highest for one-day forward returns and fades to zero by twenty days.

questions.q: What will they do before giving it capital?
options: Run it live for a month without real orders
Backtest it again on another ten years
Trade it at full size for one week first
Sell the signal to another fund for cash
questions.why: Paper trading runs the strategy on live data and logs its trades without sending orders.

lines.text: Our shorts squeezed 8% this week, and everyone has the same names on.
The longs are fine. It's the shorts dragging us.
Let's de-gross by a quarter. Cut longs and shorts together so the net doesn't change.
That takes gross from 180% to 135%.

questions.q: Gross is 180%. What is it after cutting both sides by a quarter?
questions.why: Cutting longs and shorts by a quarter cuts gross by a quarter: 180% × 0.75 = 135%.

questions.q: Why cut both sides, not just the shorts?
options: To lower risk without changing the net bet
To go net short before the squeeze ends
Because longs need more margin than shorts
Because the shorts are making money
questions.why: De-grossing shrinks the book's size while keeping its net exposure about the same.

lines.text: I want to go long the cement name. Target 20% up.
Where's your stop?
Below the March low, about 7% under the current price.
So the risk-reward is about 1:3. Start at 1% of the book and scale in. If results confirm the price hikes, size up to 3%.

questions.q: Why is the risk-reward about 1:3?
options: It risks 7% to make about 20%
It risks 20% to make about 7%
Three in four trades like it win
It is at most 3% of the book
questions.why: 7 to 20 is roughly 1 to 3.

questions.q: How does the PM want the position built?
options: Start small and add in steps if results confirm
Buy the full 3% today, before the results
Buy 1% and never add more
Buy 3% and cut it to 1% after results
questions.why: Scaling in builds the position in pieces; sizing up comes only if the thesis is confirmed.

lines.text: The pharma long is down 12%. I'd like to average down; the story hasn't changed.
It fell on a US regulator's warning letter. That changes the story.
Your stop was 8%. Don't double down on a falling knife. Cut it, and we can buy back when the facts are clear.
Understood. I'll sell it over the day.

questions.q: Why does the PM refuse to average down?
options: The news changed the reason to own it
The stock is too small for the book
Averaging down is always forbidden
The stock has already hit its target
questions.why: Averaging down only makes sense if the reason for owning the stock still holds.

questions.q: What does the trader do next?
options: Sell the position gradually through the day
Buy more of the stock at the close
Hold it and move the stop-loss lower
Hedge it by shorting Nifty futures
questions.why: 'Over the day' means spreading the order across the session.

lines.text: I bought Bank Nifty puts as a hedge for our bank longs.
How many?
About three times the delta of the longs.
Then it's not a hedge, it's a view: you're net short banks. Size it to the longs, or bring it to me as a short idea.

questions.q: Why does the PM call it a view?
options: The puts leave the book net short banks
The puts cover none of the bank risk
Puts can never be used as hedges
The puts expire before the longs are sold
questions.why: Three times the delta more than offsets the longs, so the book now profits from banks falling.

questions.q: What does the PM ask for?
options: Hedge only the longs' size, or pitch a short
Buy even more puts for extra protection
Sell the longs and keep the puts
Swap the puts for Bank Nifty calls
questions.why: A hedge should match the risk it covers; anything more is a fresh bet to be judged on its own.

lines.text: We're dollar-neutral, so why did we lose 2% when the market fell 3%?
The longs are high-beta mid caps, about 1.3. The shorts are low-beta large caps, about 0.6.
So we were net long beta.
Yes. To be beta-neutral we'd need about twice as many rupees short as long.

questions.q: Why did a dollar-neutral book lose in the fall?
options: Its longs had higher beta than its shorts
Its shorts had higher beta than its longs
It held more rupees long than short
Its stop-losses failed in the fall
questions.why: Equal rupees each side, but the longs move 1.3 times the market and the shorts only 0.6 times.

questions.q: For ₹100 crore long at beta 1.3, about how much short at beta 0.6 is beta-neutral?
options: About ₹217 crore
About ₹100 crore
About ₹46 crore
About ₹130 crore
questions.why: 100 × 1.3 = 130 of beta exposure; 130 ÷ 0.6 ≈ ₹217 crore.

lines.text: The small-cap long is ₹40 crore. It trades about ₹8 crore a day.
At 20% participation, how long to get out?
₹1.6 crore a day, so 25 days to liquidate. Our limit is five.
Then we cut it to ₹8 crore over the next two weeks, and nothing that thin goes in again.

questions.q: How many days to liquidate at 20% of volume?
options: 25 days
5 days
8 days
2 days
questions.why: 20% of ₹8 crore is ₹1.6 crore a day; ₹40 crore ÷ ₹1.6 crore = 25 days.

questions.q: Why is ₹8 crore the new size?
options: That's five days of exits at 20% of volume
That's 2% of the whole book
That's the stock's daily price limit
That's half the stock's free float
questions.why: 5 days × ₹1.6 crore a day = ₹8 crore, which fits the five-day limit.

lines.text: You're at ₹1.15 crore of loss today against a ₹1 crore limit. That's a hard breach.
It's one bad gap in one name. It'll come back.
Maybe. The rule is no new risk today, and the position cut by half by 2 pm.
Understood. I'll cut it and send the post-mortem tonight.

questions.q: What has happened?
options: The day's loss went past the agreed limit
The book hit its profit target early
The exchange halted the stock
The broker made a margin call
questions.why: A limit breach is a loss or position past a limit set by the risk team.

questions.q: What must the trader do?
options: Add no risk and halve the position by 2 pm
Wait for the stock to come back
Double the position to win it back
Close every position in the book
questions.why: After a breach the trader cuts back by a deadline; hoping it comes back isn't an option.

lines.text: VaR on the options book is only ₹2 crore, but the stress loss on a 10% gap with vol doubling is ₹25 crore.
We've had a great year selling premium.
That's why VaR looks small. Short options earn steadily until they don't. Buy some tail protection or cut the size.
We'll buy far OTM puts with a month to go.

questions.q: Why does VaR look small?
options: It's built from normal days, not crashes
The book is long options in size
The book has no options in it
VaR always adds up the worst days
questions.why: VaR looks at ordinary moves; a short options book's real risk sits in rare, big moves.

questions.q: What does the PM agree to?
options: Buy cheap far OTM puts as crash protection
Sell more premium to raise the VaR
Buy at-the-money calls for a rally
Close the whole options book today
questions.why: Far OTM puts are cheap and pay off in the crash scenario the stress test describes.

lines.text: Your top three longs are all PSU banks: 28% of the book between them.
They're different banks with different stories.
One rate decision or one government headline moves all three. That's concentration risk, and the sector limit is 20%.
Fine. I'll trim the weakest one and bring the sector under 20%.

questions.q: Why does Risk treat the three banks as one bet?
options: One event can move all three together
They trade on the same exchange
They have the same share price
They have the same lot size
questions.why: Stocks exposed to the same driver behave like one big position when that driver moves.

questions.q: Which limit is the book over?
options: The cap on one sector's share of the book
The cap on how much it can lose in a day
The cap on gross exposure
The exchange's position limit
questions.why: 28% in one sector against a 20% sector limit.

lines.text: Yesterday stocks, bonds and gold all fell together. Our diversification did nothing.
Correlations went to one.
Right. So we size on crisis correlations, not calm ones, and the books near their drawdown budget cut first.
Agreed. Two books are at 7% of a 10% budget; they halve today.

questions.q: What does 'correlations went to one' mean?
options: Assets that usually differ all fell at once
One asset moved while the rest stayed calm
Two stocks merged into one
Every trade printed at the same price
questions.why: In a panic, investors sell everything, so assets that normally move apart fall together.

questions.q: Which books halve today?
options: Those close to their drawdown limit
Those with the biggest profits
Those with the fewest positions
Those trading only in the close
questions.why: A drawdown budget sets how far a book may fall from its peak before risk is cut.

lines.text: Strategy 7 sent 4,000 orders in two minutes. It usually sends 50.
Hit the kill switch on it now, then pull every order it has working.
Done. It looks like a bad price feed made it think every quote was stale.
It stays off until we've replayed the day and tested the fix.

questions.q: What does the kill switch do?
options: Cancels its orders and stops it sending more
Shuts the exchange for two minutes
Turns off the price feed for everyone
Doubles the strategy's position limits
questions.why: A kill switch cancels open orders and blocks new ones in one step.

questions.q: What does 'pull every order' mean?
options: Cancel its working orders straight away
Send them to a different exchange
Raise their prices so they fill
Book them in the back office
questions.why: To pull an order is to cancel it.

lines.text: Election results are on Tuesday, and the options desk is short a lot of premium.
The straddle implies a 4% move. Past counts have moved the index more than that.
Then I want the desk flat into the event or hedged with wings. No naked short options over the count.
We'll buy wings tonight and cut the rest by Monday's close.

questions.q: Why is Risk nervous?
options: The real move could beat the priced move
The straddle implies too big a move
Short premium gains in big moves
Results days always have low volume
questions.why: Short premium loses if the actual move is bigger than the move the options priced in.

questions.q: What does 'no naked short options' mean?
options: Every short option needs a hedge behind it
No options may be sold before 10 am
All options must be held to expiry
Options may be traded only at the close
questions.why: Naked means unhedged; buying wings turns the short options into capped-loss spreads.

lines.text: The put base has shifted up to 24,200 overnight, and the call wall is still at 24,800.
So writers expect 24,200 to 24,800?
For now. If writers start rolling the calls down, that's bearish. Watch the OI shifting through the morning.
And if 24,200 breaks?
Then the put writers are trapped, and their covering can speed up the fall.

questions.q: What range do the option writers seem to expect?
options: No range at all
questions.why: Heavy put writing marks the floor writers expect, and heavy call writing the ceiling.

questions.q: What happens if 24,200 breaks?
options: Trapped put writers may cover and push it lower
Call writers will buy and push it higher
The exchange will halt the index
The 24,200 puts will expire worthless
questions.why: Put writers losing money buy back or hedge by selling, which adds to the fall.

lines.text: The 24,600 calls are ₹3. A 100-point move could make them ₹60. Hero or zero?
Most days they go to zero. Gamma's huge into the close, so it can happen, but it's a lottery ticket.
And for us, short the 24,500 straddle?
That's exactly where a gamma blast hurts. Our stop is 30 points on the straddle; respect it.

questions.q: Why could the ₹3 calls jump so much?
options: Gamma is very high near expiry at the money
Theta adds value in the last hour
Calls gain when volatility falls
The exchange adds time value at 3 pm
questions.why: Close to expiry, a small index move swings delta fast, so cheap near-the-money options can multiply.

questions.q: What is the risk for the short straddle?
options: A sharp late move can blow through it
It loses money if the market is quiet
It can lose only its premium
It expires worthless whatever happens
questions.why: A short straddle is short gamma: a sudden big move late on expiry day causes big losses.

lines.text: The 9:20 straddle got stopped on both legs again: calls at 10:05, puts at 1:40.
So the market went up and then down?
Exactly, a whipsaw day. Each stop hit, and neither leg earned enough decay to cover it.
That's three this week. Is it a regime change or noise?
Five days is a small sample. Let's look at the month before we change the rules.

questions.q: Why did the straddle lose?
options: The market rose then fell, hitting both stops
The market stayed flat all day
IV fell sharply after the open
The trader forgot to place the stops
questions.why: A whipsaw hits the call leg's stop on the way up and the put leg's stop on the way down.

questions.q: Why not change the rules yet?
options: A week is too little data to judge
Rules can only change at expiry
The strategy made money all week
The exchange must approve the change
questions.why: Five days is a small sample; a few bad days can be chance.

lines.text: The event's done and vol is offered. ATM IV dropped from 18 to 13 in an hour.
IV crush. What about the wings?
Skew is still bid. People are keeping their downside puts.
So the puts are rich against the ATM options. Any trade on that is a view on skew, not on direction.

questions.q: What does 'vol is offered' mean here?
options: Option sellers are pushing IV down
Brokers are offering cheap options data
Volume is very light after the event
A big seller is offering futures
questions.why: More sellers than buyers of options drive implied volatility lower.

questions.q: What does 'skew is still bid' mean?
options: OTM puts still carry high IV versus ATM
OTM calls are pricier than OTM puts
ATM options are pricier than the wings
Futures trade above the index
questions.why: Demand for downside protection keeps out-of-the-money put IV high compared with at-the-money IV.

lines.text: I wanted to sell one more straddle, but the margin blocked is already ₹3 lakh a lot.
Buy wings and the margin falls a lot, because the loss is capped.
Doesn't that cost premium?
Some. But naked selling into a long weekend isn't worth the margin or the gap risk.

questions.q: Why would buying wings cut the margin?
options: The worst-case loss is capped
Brokers refund the wings' premium
Wings make the trade risk-free
Margins are lower on Fridays
questions.why: Margin follows the worst-case loss, and the bought wings cap it.

questions.q: What does buying wings cost?
options: Some of the premium collected
A higher margin requirement
Unlimited loss on a big move
A ban on selling more options
questions.why: The wings are bought with part of the premium earned from the options sold.

lines.text: Positional view: it's a sell-on-rise market below 24,300 while FPIs keep selling.
So we short bounces into 24,300 with a stop above?
Yes. And watch the trapped longs from last week's breakout; they'll sell any bounce.
How long do we hold?
Until the series ends or the stop goes. It's NRML, not intraday.

questions.q: What does 'sell on rise' mean?
options: Use rallies to sell in a weak market
Sell only after a 5% rise
Buy every dip in an uptrend
Sell everything at the day's high
questions.why: In a downtrend, bounces are treated as chances to sell or go short.

questions.q: Why will trapped longs sell bounces?
options: They bought higher and want out near cost
Their brokers are forcing them to buy more
They earn decay on every bounce
They need margin for new longs
questions.why: Traders stuck in losing longs often sell as soon as the price gets back near where they bought.

lines.text: Buy 5 lakh Tata Steel today against VWAP. No rush.
Will do. Max participation?
15%, and don't pay above 152.
Update: 40% done at 150.40, against a VWAP of 150.55. Working the rest over the day.

questions.q: How many shares are left to buy after the update?
options: 3 lakh
2 lakh
4 lakh
1 lakh
questions.why: 40% of 5 lakh is 2 lakh done, so 3 lakh are left.

questions.q: Is the fill so far good against the benchmark?
options: Yes: buying below VWAP is better
No: buying below VWAP is a cost
No: it should match VWAP exactly
It can't be compared with VWAP
questions.why: For a buy, an average price below VWAP beats the benchmark.

lines.text: It's running away: up 1.8% since arrival, and I'm only 30% done.
News?
A big buyer, I think. Someone's lifting every offer.
Results are tomorrow and I want it all. Pay up, finish by 2 pm, and tell me the bips versus arrival.

questions.q: What does 'running away' mean here?
options: The price is rising away from the buy order
The client has cancelled the order
The stock has hit its upper circuit
The trader has left the desk
questions.why: The price is moving fast in the direction that makes the order harder to fill.

questions.q: Why does the PM say 'pay up'?
options: Finishing now matters more than the price
The price matters more than finishing
The broker's fees are due today
The order must be done at the close
questions.why: With results tomorrow, the risk of not finishing outweighs the cost of a worse price.

lines.text: Bid 612 with 80,000 shares ahead of us, offer 612.30. Should I cross the spread?
No rush on this one. Join the bid with 10,000 and see if we get filled.
And if the queue doesn't move?
Then improve the bid by a tick. We'll be first in line and still not pay the full spread.

questions.q: What does 'join the bid' mean?
options: Rest a buy at the best bid and wait
Buy straight away at the offer
Bid one tick above the best bid
Cancel the bid and wait
questions.why: Joining the bid means placing a passive buy at the current best bid, behind the queue.

questions.q: Why improve the bid instead of crossing?
options: To go first without paying the full spread
To make the trade settle a day earlier
To hide the order from other traders
To trade at the closing price
questions.why: One tick higher makes you the best bid, which costs less than buying at the offer.

lines.text: We have IOIs from two funds that might sell 10 lakh HDFC Bank.
Is either a natural? Our client wants to buy 8 lakh.
The first one is: a long-only fund cutting its weight, not a market maker.
Then let's cross it as a block at a firm price near the last trade, before word leaks.

questions.q: What is an IOI?
options: A sign a firm may trade a block, not an order
A firm order that must be filled
A report of futures open interest
An order sent to the opening auction
questions.why: An indication of interest says a client may trade in size; price and size still have to be agreed.

questions.q: Why does the trader want to move quickly?
options: Word of the block could leak and move the price
The client has asked to pay up for speed today
The fund's shares are pledged
Naturals must be filled before noon
questions.why: Information leakage: once others hear of a big seller, the price can move before the trade is done.

lines.text: It's 3:10. We've done 7 of the 10 lakh. What do you want to do with the residual?
Put half of it in the close. The rest is done for the day; start again at tomorrow's open.
Got it. I'll write the ticket for today's fills and send you the average price.
And allocate it 60-40 between the two funds.

questions.q: How many shares go into the close?
options: 1.5 lakh
3 lakh
3.5 lakh
5 lakh
questions.why: The residual is 3 lakh (10 − 7), and half of it is 1.5 lakh.

questions.q: What does 'done for the day' mean for the rest?
options: Stop for today and carry it to tomorrow
Fill it straight away at the market
Give it all to the second fund
Trade it in the closing auction
questions.why: Trading stops for today and the remainder starts again at the next open.

lines.text: Last month we were 18 bips versus arrival on average, against 11 for the algo benchmark.
Most of it came from three urgent orders where we paid up into results.
Fine, but the patient orders were 9 bips worse too. Did we front-load them?
Yes, the default schedule front-loads. We'll switch the no-rush orders to follow the volume curve.

questions.q: What is the review comparing?
options: Average fills against prices on arrival
Brokerage against last month's
Closing prices against opening prices
Orders sent against orders filled
questions.why: Bips versus arrival compares the average fill with the price when the order came in.

questions.q: Why would front-loading hurt patient orders?
options: It trades more early, paying more impact
It leaves the order unfinished at the close
It trades only in the closing auction
It skips the busy hours of the day
questions.why: Trading a big share of the order early means taking more of the market's volume, which moves the price more.

lines.text: Colour this morning: long-only funds are buying IT on the dip; hedge funds are selling banks.
Any size?
We printed a ₹400 crore block in a private bank at the open, 2% below the last close.
Who's on the other side of that? If it's a promoter selling stake, I'd wait for the rest of the supply to clear.

questions.q: What is 'colour' on a broker call?
options: A summary of who's buying and selling
A chart's red and green candles
A broker's rating on a stock
The broker's commission rate
questions.why: Market colour is the sales desk's read of the flows they are seeing.

questions.q: Why does the PM ask who's on the other side?
options: A big seller may have more still to sell
To book the trade with the right custodian
Because buyers must report every block
To ask for a discount on brokerage
questions.why: If a large holder is cutting a stake, more selling may follow and weigh on the price.

lines.text: We're axed to sell a mid-cap pharma name; a client has 15 lakh shares to go.
Indicative or firm?
Indicative around 1,180, with the stock at 1,205. Firm if you show size.
Show them firm at 1,170 for 5 lakh, subject to my risk sign-off.

questions.q: What does 'axed to sell' mean?
options: The broker has a client keen to sell
The broker cut its rating to sell
The stock was removed from an index
The broker is short the stock itself
questions.why: An axe is a strong interest to trade one way, here a selling client.

questions.q: What does 'indicative' mean here?
options: A rough price, not a commitment
A price fixed until the close
The exchange's official price
A price set by the regulator
questions.why: An indicative price is a guide; a firm price is one you can trade on.

lines.text: We're upgrading the cement name to buy, with a target of 2,400, up from 2,050.
What's the upside from here?
About 18%. Downside to our bear case is 10%.
So nearly 2 to 1. The street has it at hold, so if you're right there's a re-rating to come.

questions.q: What is the reward-to-risk on these numbers?
options: About 1.8 to 1
About 1 to 1.8
About 2.4 to 1
About 1 to 1
questions.why: 18% of upside against 10% of downside is 1.8 to 1.

questions.q: What does 're-rating' mean here?
options: The market paying a higher multiple for it
The broker repeating the same rating
The stock moving to a new index
A fall in the firm's credit rating
questions.why: A re-rating is a change in the valuation multiple investors are willing to pay.

lines.text: Index rebalance at the end of the month: two names added, one dropped.
How big is the passive demand?
About 12 days of average volume in the smaller addition, and it all trades in the close on the day.
Then it's a crowded trade by now. Everyone has bought ahead; I'd sell some to the index funds in the close.

questions.q: Why does passive demand matter?
options: Index funds must buy, whatever the price
Index funds may skip the purchase
It lowers the stock's volatility for good
It moves the stock out of F&O
questions.why: Funds that track the index have to own the new member, so their buying is predictable.

questions.q: What does the PM plan to do?
options: Sell some stock to index funds at the close
Buy the addition at the open
Short the Nifty future for the next week
Wait for the next rebalance
questions.why: If others have already bought ahead, the forced buying at the close is a chance to sell.

lines.text: The stock's up 14% on no news. The shorts are getting squeezed.
Is it near the F&O ban?
Close. Open interest is at 92% of the market-wide limit.
If it goes into the ban, nobody can add positions, only cut them. Squeezes near the ban get messy. Stay away.

questions.q: What is happening to the shorts?
options: Rising prices are forcing them to buy back
They are adding to their shorts as it rises
The exchange is closing them out
They are being paid to hold
questions.why: In a short squeeze, losses force shorts to buy back, which pushes the price higher still.

questions.q: What happens in the F&O ban?
options: No new positions, only cutting existing ones
The exchange closes every open position at once
Trading in the stock is halted
Only new shorts are allowed
questions.why: In the ban period, F&O positions in the stock can only be reduced.

lines.text: On the concall, management guided margins down 100 bps for the year.
That's a miss against the street. Where's it indicated?
About 6% lower in the pre-open.
We're underweight, so this helps us against the benchmark. I won't cover yet; analysts will be cutting estimates for a week.

questions.q: Why does the fall help the fund?
options: It holds less of the stock than the benchmark
It holds more of the stock than the benchmark
It bought puts on the stock
It sold the stock before the call
questions.why: Being underweight means a fall in the stock hurts the benchmark more than the fund.

questions.q: Why does the PM wait before covering?
options: Estimate cuts may push the stock lower
The stock can't trade in the pre-open
Underweights must be held to year end
The call raised the margin guidance
questions.why: Lower margin guidance usually leads to earnings downgrades, which can weigh on the price for days.

lines.text: Budget at 11. The straddle is pricing a 2.5% move.
Any change to STT on F&O is the big risk for the brokers we own.
And capital gains tax. Both are headline risks; we won't know until the speech.
Then we keep the book small. I'd rather be flat into the event on the brokers and buy back after.

questions.q: What does the 2.5% straddle tell you?
options: The move the options market expects
The most the index can move today
The tax the Budget may add
The straddle's return so far
questions.why: The at-the-money straddle's price is a quick read of the move the market is pricing.

questions.q: Why stay flat on the brokers into the speech?
options: A tax change could gap them either way
Brokers can't trade on Budget day
Brokers always fall on Budget day
The straddle is too cheap to buy
questions.why: STT on F&O feeds straight into brokers' volumes, so one line in the speech can move them sharply.

lines.text: The RBI cut the repo rate by 25 bps but changed the stance to neutral.
So a cut with a hawkish tone. Bonds rallied, then sold off.
Banks?
Whipsawed: up 1% on the cut, down 1% on the stance. Classic sell the news.

questions.q: Why did bonds rally and then sell off?
options: The cut was good news; the stance less so
The RBI raised rates straight after the cut
Bonds don't react to policy
The cut was bigger than expected
questions.why: A neutral stance suggests fewer cuts ahead, which took back some of the rally.

questions.q: What does 'whipsawed' mean?
options: Moved sharply one way, then the other
Moved steadily in one direction
Didn't trade at all
Rose to the upper circuit
questions.why: A whipsaw is a quick move one way followed by a reversal.

lines.text: Results beat on revenue and margins, and the stock's down 4%.
How can it fall on a beat?
It rallied 15% into the number and buyers wanted more. The beat was priced in.
And the straddle implied 6%, so anyone who bought it lost money even on a 4% move.

questions.q: Why did the stock fall on a beat?
options: Expectations were higher and it had run up
Revenue and margins missed estimates
The results came out a day late
The stock was moved out of F&O
questions.why: When a good result is already in the price, the stock can fall on the news.

questions.q: Why did straddle buyers lose on a 4% move?
options: The straddle had priced in a 6% move
Straddles lose whenever a stock falls
IV rose after the results
Straddles pay only on up moves
questions.why: A long straddle needs a move bigger than its price; after the event, implied vol also collapses.

lines.text: US markets fell 4% overnight. GIFT Nifty points to a 2% gap-down.
It's risk-off everywhere. Even the long-short book lost money; correlations went to one.
Do we sell into the open?
No panic selling. We have dry powder. Let the first hour settle, then buy the names we like at a discount.

questions.q: What does 'risk-off' mean?
options: Investors are dumping risky assets for safety
The risk team has stopped checking limits
The exchange has halted trading
Volatility has fallen sharply
questions.why: In a risk-off move, money leaves stocks and other risky assets for safer ones.

questions.q: What does the head of desk plan to do?
options: Wait, then use spare cash to buy
Sell everything at the open
Short the market with all spare cash
Close the book until the US recovers
questions.why: Dry powder is cash or risk kept back for moments like this.

lines.text: It's 2:45 and we're short the 24,500 straddle, with the index at 24,520.
Pin risk?
Yes. Near the strike, a small move flips which leg ends in the money. I'd rather close it than babysit it to 3:30.
Even if we give up the last of the decay?
There's ₹4 of decay left. The gamma risk is ten times that.

questions.q: What is the risk the trader worries about?
options: A small move near the strike decides the payoff
The options get exercised early
Volume dries up in the last hour
The straddle gains value as time passes
questions.why: Pin risk is the uncertainty when the price sits right at a short strike near expiry.

questions.q: Why give up the last of the decay?
options: A late move could cost far more than ₹4
Decay is zero on expiry day
Option trading stops at 2:45
The straddle can't lose more than ₹4
questions.why: The little time value left isn't worth the risk of a sharp late move.

lines.text: We gapped down 2% at the open. My stop at 24,300 filled at 24,050.
That's gap risk. Your stop protects you during the day, not over a weekend.
Should I buy it back here?
Only if the reason for the trade still holds. Otherwise don't revenge trade; you're done for the day.

questions.q: Why did the stop fill so far below 24,300?
options: The market opened below it, skipping the level
The broker delayed the order on purpose
Stops fill only at the day's low
The exchange moved the stop overnight
questions.why: A stop triggers at the first price available, and after a gap that can be well past the stop.

questions.q: What does 'revenge trade' mean?
options: Trading to win back a loss quickly
Trading against a rival desk
Trading only on Mondays
Reversing a trade a client disputes
questions.why: Revenge trading is trading bigger or faster right after a loss to get the money back.
